newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris court sends Papon to trial for war crimes.
newsitem.headline: Paris court sends Papon to trial for war crimes.

text.p: The French Supreme Court on Thursday ordered former cabinet minister Maurice Papon to stand trial on charges of crimes against humanity for deporting 1,560 Jews, including many children, to Nazi death camps in 1942-44.
The trial by jury in a Bordeaux assize court, after a legal marathon of more than 15 years, will probably be France's last chance to put wartime Nazi collaboration in the dock.
In a last-ditch bid to avoid trial, Papon, 86, had appealed to the Supreme Court after the Bordeaux appeals court ruled last September that he should stand trial.
Public prosecutors have built up a 50,000-page case against Papon, who was secretary-general of the Bordeaux prefect's office under the collaborationist Vichy government.

The Supreme Court ruled that Papon knew that deporting the Jews would lead them inevitably to their deaths. It put the number of deportees at 1,560, whereas the Bordeaux court had noted 1,690 Jews including 223 children.
Papon obeyed Nazi orders and it was irrelevant whether he believed in Nazi ideology or not, the Supreme Court found.

In a statement issued minutes after the ruling, Papon branded it strange and scandalous, adding that it would allow Communists, "the leftist lobby", state authorities and foreign institutions tying France to the Holocaust to settle old scores.
"As in all political trials, the outcome is already settled with the authorities. I will resist such dishonouring acts which recall the sad adventure of Captain Dreyfus," he said.

French Jewish army officer Alfred Dreyfus was convicted of treason in 1894 on forged evidence and jailed. He was eventually declared innocent after a bitter controversy tinged with anti-semitism which deeply split the country.

"The truth is that if the Germans pulled the strings, it was the Vichy (collaborationist regime) which carried out this policy of genocide," said Michel Slitinsky, who escaped arrest in a 1942 round-up and who found the Papon files years later.
The CRIF umbrella group for French Jewish associations said it hoped the young would learn as much from a Papon trial as from those of Hitler aide Adolf Eichman and Nazi officer Klaus Barbie.

His wartime record unknown, Papon enjoyed a meteoric post-war career, serving as Paris police chief in the 1960s and then as budget minister in the 1970s until files documenting his arrests and deportation orders were found in 1981.
After benefiting from delaying tactics by successive governments, Papon will be only the second Frenchman -- and probably the last -- tried on such charges arising from the war.

A lower-ranking collaborationist, former militia officer Paul Touvier, was jailed for life in 1994 and died in prison last year aged 81. A former police chief in the Vichy government, Rene Bousquet, was shot dead by a publicity-hungry failed writer in 1993 before he could stand trial.

The Supreme Court affirmed an earlier court ruling to give Papon a jury trial on charges of being an accomplice to the kidnapping and murder of deportees sent to Nazi death camps. Few of the deportees ever returned.
The court also upheld charges that Papon was an accomplice to arbitrary arrests, the arrest of minors under 15 years old, inhuman acts and attempted illegal arrests.
Papon has argued he helped the Resistance, saved several Jews and watered down the Vichy government's harshest orders.
Legal proceedings began in 1983, were annulled on technicalities in 1987, started again from scratch and were finally completed in June 1995.
The late President Francois Mitterrand, himself a former Vichy official, sought to prevent trials for crimes against humanity, arguing they undermined national unity.
His Gaullist successor Jacques Chirac in 1995 acknowledged the French state's responsibility in the deportation of the Jews, the first post-war leader to do so.
